nodes.label: Mountain weather
nodes.answer: Check a current mountain-specific forecast. Conditions can differ sharply from the valley, so review wind, temperature, precipitation, visibility, and hazards before setting out, and make a backup plan.

nodes.label: Wind
nodes.answer: Check both sustained wind speed and gusts, especially for exposed ridges and summits. Strong gusts can make balance, navigation, and movement difficult even when the average wind speed seems manageable.

nodes.label: Temperature
nodes.answer: Use the feels-like temperature, not only the air temperature. Wind, moisture, altitude, and darkness can make conditions feel much colder and increase the risk of hypothermia.

nodes.label: Precipitation
nodes.answer: Look at precipitation type, probability, intensity, duration, and expected accumulation. Rain can make trails slippery and streams dangerous, while snow can obscure paths and greatly reduce visibility.

nodes.label: Visibility
nodes.answer: Poor visibility makes route finding difficult and can cause disorientation, especially in fog, low cloud, or blowing snow. Carry a map, compass, and GPS, and be prepared to turn back.

nodes.label: Cloud cover
nodes.answer: Cloud cover affects temperature, visibility, and navigation. Low cloud can hide landmarks and summits, while clear skies may bring stronger nighttime cooling.

nodes.label: Freezing level
nodes.answer: The freezing level is the altitude at which air temperature reaches 0°C. If it is near or below your route, expect a transition from rain to snow, icy surfaces, and colder feels-like temperatures.

nodes.label: Thunderstorms
nodes.answer: Avoid exposed ridges, summits, and open terrain when thunderstorms are likely. Start early, watch cloud development, and choose a safe descent or shelter option before conditions deteriorate.

nodes.label: Snow and ice
nodes.answer: Snow and ice can hide the trail, make footing unreliable, and increase navigation difficulty. Use appropriate traction, insulation, and navigation tools, and reassess the route if conditions are worse than forecast.

nodes.label: Avalanche risk
nodes.answer: In winter, check the regional avalanche bulletin in addition to the weather forecast. Avoid known avalanche terrain when danger is elevated, and base route choices on slope angle, snowpack, and recent weather.

nodes.label: Mountain and valley winds
nodes.answer: Mountain terrain creates local wind patterns: heated air often moves upslope during the day, while cooler air drains downhill at night. These winds can change temperature, cloud formation, and fire behavior.

nodes.label: Foehn effect
nodes.answer: A foehn is a warm, dry wind descending the lee side of a mountain range. It can cause rapid temperature rises, very low humidity, and strong or gusty conditions.

nodes.label: Weather warnings
nodes.answer: Treat official weather warnings as a planning threshold, not optional information. If a warning covers your route or time window, postpone, choose a lower alternative, or turn back early.

nodes.label: Mountain forecast checklist
nodes.answer: Before a mountain trip, check wind and gusts, feels-like temperature, precipitation, visibility, freezing level, sunrise and sunset, and official warnings. Identify a turnaround time and a lower or shorter backup route.

nodes.label: Clothing layers
nodes.answer: Use a layering system: a moisture-wicking base layer, insulating mid layer, and wind- and water-resistant shell. Carry extra insulation, gloves, a hat, and dry clothes for delays or worsening weather.

nodes.label: Turnaround time
nodes.answer: Set a turnaround time before leaving and respect it even if the summit is close. Weather, fatigue, darkness, and route conditions can change faster than expected in mountains.

nodes.label: Humidity
nodes.answer: High humidity reduces evaporative cooling, so hot and humid conditions can increase heat illness risk. It can also contribute to fog, condensation, and wet gear.

nodes.label: Dew point
nodes.answer: Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and moisture begins to condense. A dew point close to the air temperature often means humid, muggy conditions and a higher chance of fog or dew.

nodes.label: Air pressure
nodes.answer: Falling pressure can signal an approaching low-pressure system and deteriorating weather. Rising pressure is more often associated with settling conditions, though local terrain can modify both.

nodes.label: UV index
nodes.answer: UV exposure increases with altitude and can be intensified by reflection from snow. Use sunscreen, sunglasses, a hat, and shade, even on cool or cloudy days.

nodes.label: Daylight and twilight
nodes.answer: Plan your route around sunrise, sunset, and twilight. Darkness increases navigation difficulty and cold stress, so carry a headlamp and set a turnaround time with enough margin.

nodes.label: Altitude effect
nodes.answer: Temperature generally falls as elevation increases, so summit conditions can be much colder and windier than at the trailhead. Check an elevation-specific forecast rather than relying on the valley forecast.

nodes.label: Rain shadow
nodes.answer: Mountains can force moist air to rise and release precipitation on the windward side, leaving the downwind side drier. Nearby areas can therefore have very different weather at the same time.

nodes.label: Orographic clouds
nodes.answer: Air forced upward by mountains can form clouds directly over ridges and summits. Rapidly building or persistent summit clouds can indicate strengthening wind, moisture, or an approaching weather change.

nodes.label: Hypothermia
nodes.answer: Hypothermia can occur in any season when cold, wind, and wet clothing combine. Watch for uncontrollable shivering, clumsiness, confusion, or fatigue; stop, shelter from wind, remove wet layers, and warm the person.

nodes.label: Heat illness
nodes.answer: In heat, start early, rest in shade, drink regularly, and replace electrolytes. Stop and cool down if someone develops headache, nausea, fatigue, cramps, confusion, or reduced sweating.

nodes.label: Flash flood
nodes.answer: Avoid narrow canyons, gullies, and stream crossings during or after heavy rain. Water levels can rise quickly, so move to higher ground and never attempt to cross fast-moving water.

nodes.label: Whiteout
nodes.answer: In a whiteout, visual references disappear and route finding becomes extremely difficult. Navigate by compass bearing and known features, stay on a marked route if possible, and turn back early if visibility continues to fall.

nodes.label: Lightning safety
nodes.answer: If lightning threatens, leave summits, ridges, open ground, isolated trees, and water. Move to lower terrain with denser smaller trees, avoid shallow caves and overhangs, remove exposed metal, and keep the group spaced out.

nodes.label: Rapid weather change
nodes.answer: Mountain weather can deteriorate quickly, especially in the afternoon. Watch for building clouds, rising wind, falling temperature, and falling pressure; be ready to shorten or abandon the route.

nodes.label: Go or no-go decision
nodes.answer: Make a go or no-go decision using the forecast, official warnings, route exposure, daylight, group experience, and available escape options. If key conditions are uncertain or worse than planned, choose a safer alternative.

nodes.label: Emergency weather plan
nodes.answer: Identify escape routes, shelter options, and communication coverage before departure. Carry navigation tools, insulation, a first-aid kit, and a way to call for help; share your plan and expected return time.
